On your own Wi-Fi none of this is used: the Monitor phone carries the session itself and nothing leaves the house. These fields only matter for watching from somewhere else, which needs a small always-on service to introduce the two phones — and, when neither can be reached directly, a TURN relay to forward the media.

Nothing here ever records or keeps your camera or microphone. A rendezvous only introduces the two phones. A TURN relay forwards a stream that stays encrypted end to end, so it cannot see inside it and keeps nothing.

Leave a field empty to use Tawny’s own. If your relay cannot be reached, the app falls back to Tawny’s rather than failing — a wrong address here costs a few seconds, not a working app.

Then leave every field on this screen blank — the container needs nothing from here. It finds this phone on your own network by itself. These fields are only for pointing the app at your own rendezvous when you are not using the container.

A separate concern from Rendezvous above: these only matter if the two phones can’t already reach each other directly once introduced. If they share a private network — the same Wi-Fi, or the same Tailscale tailnet — that’s already true, and both fields below can stay empty.

Tawny turns two spare phones into a pet camera. Leave one with your cat or dog — on a charger, pointed at their favourite spot — and keep the other with you to look in, listen, and say hello.

The picture and sound go straight from one phone to the other, scrambled so that only your two phones can read them. There is no account to make, nothing is ever recorded, and no server in between ever sees your video or the code that pairs your phones. On your own Wi-Fi, none of it leaves the house.

Tawny is free, and it stays that way — every part of it, for everyone. Looking in from outside the house hops through a small relay I run, and that relay adds up a bandwidth bill every month. If Tawny earns a place in your day, a little toward that bill means a lot. Chipping in unlocks nothing extra — no badge, no hidden features. That part is on purpose.

That last one is for anything at all — a question, a bug, something that broke. If a connection will not hold, long-press the version number on any screen first and send the little diagnostics log along with your note.
Tipping unlocks nothing — no badge, no features, nothing. It goes towards the relay that lets you watch from outside the house.

This phone has to stay awake to keep streaming, and its screen is what drains it. Three things help more than anything else:

1. Leave it on a charger.

2. Turn the screen brightness right down — and turn adaptive brightness off, or the phone will quietly brighten itself back up.

3. Once a viewer has connected, tap “Dim screen”. Tawny takes the backlight down to almost nothing and keeps streaming.

One phone stays with your pet and becomes the Monitor — an old phone on a charger is perfect. The other comes with you as the Viewer.
The Monitor shows a QR code. Point the Viewer’s camera at it, and that’s the whole setup — no account, no sign-up, nothing to type.
Watch and listen live. Hold to talk, play a chime to call them over, turn on the Monitor’s light in a dark room, or save a snapshot.

Video and sound go straight between your phones, encrypted, and nothing is ever recorded by us. Questions later? Help & feedback is on the home screen.
Answers to common questions, and a direct line to us.
A one-minute look at how Tawny works
A bug, an idea, or anything else
The log to send us if a connection won’t hold
Why do I need two phones?

One phone is the camera that stays with your pet (the Monitor); the other is the one you watch on (the Viewer). There is no cloud camera service in between — your own phones do the whole job, which is how your video stays yours.
How do I connect the two phones?

On the phone that stays home, choose “The Monitor”. It shows a QR code. On your other phone, choose “The Viewer” and scan that code. No camera on hand? On the Monitor tap “Show as link”, send it to yourself, and paste it on the Viewer. Once paired, the Viewer remembers the Monitor.
Can I watch when I’m not at home?
Yes. Tawny connects the two phones over the internet by itself — nothing to set up and no ports to open. The first time you connect from away, check that the short safety code matches on both phones.
Why does the Monitor stop when its screen turns off?

Android takes the camera away from any app that isn’t on screen, so the Monitor has to stay open. If it does get interrupted, the Viewer shows “Monitor paused” and the picture comes back as soon as Tawny is open again. To save power, use “Dim screen” instead of switching the screen off.
How do I save battery on the Monitor?
Keep it on a charger, turn the brightness down and adaptive brightness off, and tap “Dim screen” once a Viewer has connected. The backlight goes almost completely dark while the stream keeps running.
Is my video recorded or stored anywhere?

No. Video and sound travel encrypted, directly between your phones, and are never recorded or kept by us. There’s no account, no ads and no analytics. Snapshots and clips you save yourself stay on your phone, in Pictures/Tawny and Movies/Tawny.
Can more than one person watch?
Up to three phones can watch one Monitor at the same time. On the Monitor, tap the + in the corner to show the pairing code again and scan it from the new phone.
Why can’t I turn on the light?

The light is the Monitor’s camera flash, so the Monitor has to be using its back camera — switch it with “Flip camera”. Some phones and most tablets have no flash at all. The light turns itself off after five minutes to spare the Monitor’s battery.
The phones won’t connect. What can I try?

Make sure Tawny is open on both phones and both are online — Wi-Fi at either end helps. Pairing codes expire after ten minutes, so scan a fresh one. Still stuck? Send us the connection diagnostics from the “Tell us” section below.
No. Tawny is free, with no ads and nothing to unlock. You can chip in toward the relay it runs on, but it gets you nothing extra — on purpose.
Pick what it is and tell us in a few words. It opens in your email app, so you can check it before it’s sent.
What happened, or what would make Tawny better?
No email app — note copied. Paste it to %1$s
Only your servers. Every fallback off. You set every connection.
Off — Tawny’s servers and public STUN stay behind yours as a safety net.
On — nothing falls back. If something here is wrong or down, watching from outside your Wi-Fi will not work at all.

With this on, this phone contacts only the servers you type on this screen, and nothing else:

• No Tawny rendezvous. If yours is wrong, down or unreachable, remote watching stops. Nothing takes over.
• No public STUN. Blank STUN means none at all, and on some networks that means no connection.
• No relay picked up from a scanned code, and no “Send to Tawny” for diagnostics.
• Leave Rendezvous blank and the phones can only meet on your own Wi-Fi.

Both phones need the same settings. Tawny cannot tell a broken setup apart from one you meant, so it will not warn you mid-call or fix it for you. You are fully in control, and so is fixing it.

Your video and sound stay encrypted end to end either way. This changes who you depend on to connect, not whether anyone can watch.

Tighter privacy is on. This phone uses exactly what is on this screen and nothing else: no Tawny server, no public STUN, no fallback of any kind.\n\nBlank means none. A blank Rendezvous means the phones only meet on your own Wi-Fi. Blank STUN means no STUN.

STUN lets each phone learn its public address, and TURN forwards media when no direct path works. Under tighter privacy only the servers you list here are used. Leave STUN blank to send no STUN request anywhere, which usually rules out connecting between two different networks unless you use a VPN or TURN.
What this phone may do to reach the other one. Each option below can take away a way of connecting. That is your call.
Direct first. The relay carries the stream only if the phones cannot reach each other.
Every call goes through your TURN relay. Neither phone ever learns the other’s IP address. Needs a TURN server that works, or nothing connects.
No relay, ever. Only direct connections, so two strict networks (carrier NAT on both ends) will not connect.
Fetch short-lived TURN credentials from the rendezvous above, as Tawny’s own relay does. Off: only the TURN servers typed here.
The Monitor runs a small relay on your Wi-Fi and puts its address in the pairing code. Off: nothing listens on the phone, the code has no address, and every session goes through your rendezvous.
Takes effect on the next session. Nothing here is checked against a live server. A wrong address shows up as a call that does not connect.
With the direct Wi-Fi path off, this is the only way the phones can meet. Add a rendezvous, or turn the Wi-Fi path back on.
“Always” relays every call, so it needs a TURN server: add one here, or let your rendezvous hand one out.
From the next session this phone contacts only:
Direct Wi-Fi path: off (nothing listens on this phone)
Your rendezvous is ws://, which is not encrypted. Use it only on a network you trust.
No Tawny server, no public STUN, no fallback. Put the same settings on the other phone. If a call does not connect, the cause is in this list.
Your addresses are cleared from this phone and tighter privacy is turned off. Tawny’s servers and public STUN come back as the fallback.

Tighter privacy is on, and this phone has no way to reach the other one: no rendezvous is set, and there is no direct Wi-Fi path (it is turned off, or this pairing has no Wi-Fi address).\n\nThis is deliberate. With every fallback off, Tawny will not pick a server for you. Add your rendezvous, or turn the Wi-Fi path back on, in Servers.
